svg.aria-label: Diagram: how an Azure RBAC role assignment is built from a security principal, a role definition and a scope, the nine-step evaluation order Azure Resource Manager follows from token to allowed or denied including deny assignments winning first and effective permissions computed as Actions minus NotActions, the additive model in which a Contributor assignment at subscription scope and a Reader assignment on a resource group sum to Contributor, and the separation between control plane and data plane permissions with the per-scope assignment limits
svg.title: Azure RBAC: three elements make an assignment, permissions add up rather than narrow, and control plane access does not reach the data
svg.text: RBAC looks like Policy and behaves like its opposite.
Same three-part shape, same hierarchy, same inheritance — but assignments add up instead of layering most-restrictive, and nothing here subtracts.
A role assignment is exactly three things
Security principal
User, group, service principal
or managed identity.
Group assignments are transitive:
a group inside a group inherits.
Role definition
Actions, NotActions, DataActions,
NotDataActions, AssignableScopes.
NotActions is not a deny rule.
Another role granting it wins.
Scope
Management group, subscription, resource
group or resource. Lower levels inherit
role permissions from higher levels.
The assignment is an extension resource.
How Resource Manager decides — the order matters more than the roles do
1. The principal acquires a token for Resource Manager,
including transitive group memberships.
2. ARM retrieves every role assignment and deny
assignment that applies to the resource.
3. If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked.
4. Otherwise the roles for this principal are narrowed
to this resource.
5. Actions − NotActions = effective permissions.
DataActions − NotDataActions, separately.
6. Any conditions on the assignment are evaluated,
up to 8 KB of them. Then allow, or deny.
Additive: your permissions are the sum
There is no narrowing. A tighter assignment lower down
does not reduce a broader one above it.
Contributor
on the subscription
Reader
on one resource group
= Contributor everywhere in the subscription
The Reader assignment has no effect at all. To reduce what
someone can do, remove the broader assignment — adding a
narrower one is not a restriction, it is a no-op.
Two planes, and a wildcard that does not cross between them
Control plane
Actions / NotActions — manage the storage account, create a container, delete a resource group
Data plane
DataActions / NotDataActions — read a blob, write a blob, delete a message in a queue
Owner at subscription scope still cannot read a blob by default.
The separation is what stops a wildcard becoming data access.
The budgets, and the delays that make RBAC feel broken when it is not
4,000 role assignments per subscription · 500 per management group · 5,000 custom roles per tenant · 2,000 assignable scopes per custom role
and exactly one management group among them · condition up to 8 KB · 2,000 system-managed deny assignments per subscription
Assigning or removing a role can take up to 10 minutes to take effect, at every scope. Signing out and back in forces the refresh.
For a managed identity added to a group, the back-end cache is held per resource URI for around 24 hours — hours, not minutes.
A built-in role with DataActions assigned at management group scope may take several hours to reach the data plane.
Sources: Azure RBAC overview, role definitions, scope overview, troubleshooting, and Azure subscription and service limits, on Microsoft Learn.
